title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 315: The Loom of Reason: Weaving and Early Computing
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 315 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Loom of Reason: Weaving, Mathematics, and Early Computing

Paragraph 1. Most books say computer history began in the 1940s with war scientists like Alan Turing. However, technology writer Dr. Miranda Croft shares a very different story. She explains that the main idea of computer software actually started in early 1800s weaving shops. The first person to separate a machine from its instructions was a French silk weaver named Joseph Marie Jacquard.

Paragraph 2. In 1804, Jacquard built a clever new weaving machine, called a loom. Before his invention, a young helper had to pull hundreds of threads up and down by hand all day. That old way was very slow and caused many mistakes. Jacquard changed this by joining thick paper cards together in a long chain. Small holes punched in each card told the machine which threads to lift. By changing the paper cards, one loom could weave completely different flower pictures automatically.

Paragraph 3. Later, in the 1830s, English thinker Charles Babbage saw how smart Jacquard's cards were. Babbage was designing the Analytical Engine, an early idea for a general computer. He decided to use Jacquard's punched cards to give math steps to his machine. Mathematician Ada Lovelace worked closely with Babbage. She saw that computers could work not only with numbers, but also with music, letters, and rules.

Paragraph 4. Sadly, neither Babbage nor Lovelace ever finished building a working Analytical Engine. Old factory machines in the 1800s could not cut metal parts accurately enough. Still, Dr. Croft reminds us that our modern digital world grew directly out of simple cloth weaving.
